title: “GIVE TO EVERYONE WHO ASKS” — DID JESUS REALLY MEAN A CHRISTIAN CAN NEVER SAY NO?
paragraphs:
“GIVE TO EVERYONE WHO ASKS” — DID JESUS REALLY MEAN A CHRISTIAN CAN NEVER SAY NO?
What if the most Christlike answer to someone asking for your money is sometimes “yes”… sometimes “not like that”… and sometimes a heartbreaking “no”?
There is a sentence from Jesus that can make a tenderhearted Christian feel guilty almost immediately.
Someone asks you for money.
You hesitate.
Then the verse enters your mind.
“Give to everyone who asks you…”
Luke 6:30.
And suddenly your hesitation feels like sin.
So you give.
Again.
Maybe you give money you really cannot afford to lose.
Maybe you help someone whose behavior has not changed because everyone keeps rescuing them from its consequences.
Maybe you lend to a relative who has broken promise after promise.
Maybe somebody discovers that you are a Christian and begins using your compassion as leverage.
“You’re supposed to help people.”
“Aren’t Christians supposed to give?”
“What would Jesus do?”
And now you are trapped between two fears.
If you say yes, you may be enabling something destructive.
If you say no, you wonder whether you have just disobeyed Jesus.
But what if the question is deeper than, “Must Christians always say yes?”
What if Jesus is confronting something far more dangerous than the word no?
What if He is confronting the clenched fist of a heart that has stopped loving?
Listen carefully to the actual words preserved for us in the Greek text of Luke 6:30:
“παντὶ αἰτοῦντί σε δίδου”
panti aitounti se didou.
A straightforward rendering is:
“Give to everyone asking you.”
The command is real.
We should not weaken it simply because it makes us uncomfortable.
Jesus really does call His disciples to radical generosity.
But we also should not tear one sentence out of the sermon in which Jesus spoke it and turn it into a mechanical rule that the rest of Scripture never teaches.
Because Jesus was not training His disciples to become human vending machines.
He was teaching them to become people whose lives had been conquered by grace.
Look at what surrounds the command.
Jesus says to love your enemies.
Do good to those who hate you.
Bless those who curse you.
Pray for those who mistreat you.
Give without living with your fist permanently closed.
Treat others as you would want them to treat you.
Love people who cannot repay you.
Be merciful because your Father is merciful.
That is the atmosphere surrounding “Give to everyone who asks.”
This is not primarily a lesson in financial transactions.
It is a revolution of the human heart.
Jesus is destroying the old mathematics of fallen humanity:
“You hurt me, so I hurt you.”
“You owe me, so I own you.”
“You cannot benefit me, so you are useless to me.”
“You took from me, so I will spend the rest of my life making you pay.”
Jesus walks directly into that world and says:
Love.
Give.
Forgive.
Show mercy.
Do good without calculating what you will receive in return.
And that changes the question completely.
The question is no longer merely:
“Do I have to give this person what they asked for?”
The deeper question becomes:
“How can I genuinely love this person before God?”
Sometimes love gives exactly what was requested.
Sometimes love gives more.
Sometimes love gives something completely different.
And sometimes love refuses to finance destruction.
Imagine someone you deeply love is destroying himself through addiction.
He asks you for cash.
You know where that money is probably going.
Does “Give to everyone who asks” mean Jesus commands you to hand him money that may help purchase the very substance destroying his body?
Or could generosity look different?
“I won't give you cash for that. But I'll buy you dinner.”
“I'll help you get home safely.”
“I'll sit with you while you call someone for help.”
“I'll help you look for treatment.”
“I'll pray with you.”
“I won't finance what is destroying you, but I am not abandoning you either.”
That is not necessarily stinginess.
That may be love refusing to disguise itself as convenience.
Because biblical love does not merely ask, “What does this person want from me right now?”
Love asks, “What actually seeks this person's good before God?”
And Scripture itself prevents us from interpreting Jesus as commanding indiscriminate compliance with every request.
Paul wrote something startling to the Thessalonian church:
“εἴ τις οὐ θέλει ἐργάζεσθαι μηδὲ ἐσθιέτω.”
ei tis ou thelei ergazesthai, mēde esthietō.
“If anyone is not willing to work, neither let him eat.”
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say that anyone who cannot work should starve.
The Greek uses θέλει — thelei.
Wills.
Wants.
Is willing.
The issue is unwillingness, not inability.
That matters enormously.
Scripture repeatedly commands compassion toward the poor, the vulnerable, the stranger, the widow, and people in genuine need.
Christian generosity should be scandalously visible.
But biblical generosity and indiscriminate enabling are not the same thing.
In fact, the same New Testament that commands generosity also commands responsibility.
Paul tells Timothy that if someone refuses to care for his own relatives—and especially his own household—he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
The Greek text says:
“εἰ δέ τις τῶν ἰδίων καὶ μάλιστα οἰκείων οὐ προνοεῖ…”
ei de tis tōn idiōn kai malista oikeiōn ou pronoei…
If someone does not provide for his own, especially those of his household…
Think about what that means.
You can give so recklessly outside your home that you neglect responsibilities God has already placed inside it.
A father cannot abandon the needs of his children and call that generosity.
A mother does not need to empty the grocery budget because somebody manipulated her with a Bible verse.
A Christian does not have to bankrupt the household to prove that he loves Jesus.
Generosity without wisdom can become irresponsibility.
And wisdom without generosity can become selfishness.
Jesus calls us to neither.
He calls us to love.
Real love.
Costly love.
Holy love.
The kind of love that cannot hide greed behind the word “wisdom.”
But also the kind that cannot hide cowardice behind the word “kindness.”
And perhaps that is where this teaching becomes uncomfortable.
Because some of us are desperate to discover when Christians are allowed to say no because, deep inside, we are looking for permission not to give.
We have more than enough.
Someone genuinely needs help.
We could help without harming them or neglecting those entrusted to us.
But we start building theological barricades around our wallets.
“What if they're irresponsible?”
“What if they're lying?”
“What if they don't deserve it?”
Be careful.
Because sooner or later the Gospel asks you a devastating question:
What did you deserve when Christ showed mercy to you?
Jesus did not wait until sinners became worthy before coming for them.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.”
That is Romans 5.
The Gospel is not the story of good people receiving their wages.
It is the story of guilty people receiving mercy.
You brought Jesus your debt.
He brought you His righteousness.
You brought Him your rebellion.
He brought you reconciliation.
You brought Him sin.
He brought you blood.
You brought Him shame.
He brought you a cross.
And at that cross, the greatest scandal in human history became the doorway to grace.
The innocent One stood where the guilty belonged.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
The King wore the crown of thorns.
The Author of life entered death.
And three days later, death discovered it had swallowed Someone it could not keep.
This is why Christian generosity cannot merely be reduced to rules about money.
We give because God gave.
We forgive because we were forgiven.
We show mercy because mercy found us.
We loosen our grip because nails once pierced the hands that refused to let us go.
But grace is not the same thing as enabling.
Jesus loved people perfectly, yet He did not comply with every demand made of Him.
People wanted signs on demand.
He sometimes refused.
People wanted to force Him into their expectations.
He withdrew.
People wanted Him to operate according to their timetable.
He did not.
Even His closest disciples sometimes wanted things that sounded reasonable but contradicted the Father's purpose.
Jesus could say no without ceasing to love.
That should free somebody reading this.
Maybe you have spent years believing that every boundary makes you selfish.
Maybe somebody taught you that Christianity means never disappointing anyone.
Maybe every request feels like a command.
Every need feels like your responsibility.
Every sad story becomes your emergency.
And whenever you cannot rescue someone, guilt begins whispering:
“If you really loved Jesus, you would fix this.”
No.
You are not the Messiah.
Jesus already occupies that position.
You are called to love people.
You are not called to become their savior.
Sometimes saying yes is obedience.
Sometimes saying no is stewardship.
Sometimes the most Christlike response is neither simply yes nor no, but:
“I cannot give you what you're asking for, but I refuse to stop caring about you.”
That sentence may cost more than handing someone twenty dollars.
Because cash can make someone disappear.
Love may require you to stay.
Maybe the hungry person does not merely need money.
Maybe he needs a meal and somebody willing to look him in the eyes.
Maybe the struggling single mother does not need another inspirational quote.
Maybe she needs groceries.
Maybe your elderly neighbor does not need your theology explained.
Maybe she needs someone to carry something heavy.
Maybe your unemployed friend does not only need another loan.
Maybe he needs encouragement, accountability, introductions, transportation, help writing a résumé, and somebody who believes his story is not over.
Sometimes the easiest thing to give is money.
Sometimes the hardest thing to give is yourself.
And Jesus has always been after more than your wallet.
He wants your heart.
That is why there is another danger hiding on the opposite side of this teaching.
You can become so afraid of “enabling” people that you slowly stop being generous at all.
Every poor person becomes suspicious.
Every request becomes manipulation.
Every act of mercy requires an investigation.
Every hurting human being has to prove that they deserve your compassion.
And before long, you have protected yourself from being exploited…
but you may also have protected yourself from being moved.
That is dangerous territory for anyone following the Man who wept.
The Man who touched lepers.
The Man who noticed beggars.
The Man who ate with people respectable religion wanted nothing to do with.
The Man who looked at crowds and felt compassion.
The Man who washed feet.
The Man who gave Himself.
Christian discernment must never become baptized indifference.
Sometimes you will give and discover later that somebody deceived you.
Sometimes your generosity will be misunderstood.
Sometimes somebody may take advantage of your kindness.
Wisdom matters.
Stewardship matters.
Boundaries can matter.
But do not allow the possibility of being used to transform you into someone who can no longer be moved.
There is something worse than occasionally giving to someone who did not deserve your generosity.
It is becoming a person who believes nobody deserves generosity unless they can earn it.
Because if God had treated us according to that standard…
where would we be?
Maybe that is the scandal underneath this entire conversation.
We desperately want to know who deserves our generosity while standing every day beneath a cross declaring that salvation itself was given to people who could never deserve it.
Grace does not mean foolishness.
Grace does not mean financing evil.
Grace does not mean surrendering every boundary.
Grace does not mean allowing manipulation.
Grace means that even your no should come from a heart that still loves.
You can refuse the request without despising the requester.
You can establish a boundary without seeking revenge.
You can stop giving cash while continuing to offer food.
You can refuse manipulation while continuing to pray.
You can say, “I cannot keep rescuing you from this consequence,” while still saying, “I will walk beside you while you rebuild.”
That is harder than either extreme.
It is easier to give everyone everything.
No discernment required.
It is also easier to give nobody anything.
No sacrifice required.
Jesus calls us somewhere deeper.
Generosity with wisdom.
Mercy with truth.
Compassion with discernment.
Grace without enabling sin.
Boundaries without bitterness.
Open hands governed by a surrendered heart.
So the next time someone asks you for something, perhaps do not begin with:
“Am I technically obligated to say yes?”
Begin here:
“Jesus, what does love require of me right now?”
Maybe He will tell you to open your wallet.
Maybe He will tell you to open your refrigerator.
Maybe He will tell you to open your home.
Maybe He will tell you to open your schedule.
Maybe He will tell you to give something far more expensive than money:
your attention.
your forgiveness.
your patience.
your presence.
Maybe He will expose the selfishness you have been calling discernment.
Or maybe He will give you courage to finally establish a boundary you have been afraid to establish.
Either way, the goal is not protecting your money.
And the goal is not proving your generosity.
The goal is becoming like Christ.
Bring it to Jesus.
There may be another believer reading who has walked through the same thing and can remind you that you are not alone.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. Grace cannot be bought.
Come to Jesus.
Because eventually the question is no longer whether you gave enough money to people who asked.
The question is whether the Christ who gave Himself for you has been given your heart.
If you have been stingy, repent.
If you have been manipulated, seek wisdom.
If you have enabled what is destroying someone you love, ask God for courage.
If bitterness has closed your hands, ask Christ to soften them again.
If you have confused being needed with being faithful, surrender that too.
You do not have to save everyone.
You cannot.
But you can point them toward the One who saves completely.
His name is Jesus.
The One who receives sinners.
The One who forgives the guilty.
The One who restores the fallen.
The One who can take the ugliest chapter of a human life and refuse to call it the ending.
Because maybe your story has some scandal in it too.
Maybe there are things you hope nobody discovers.
Maybe you have taken more than you have given.
Maybe you have manipulated.
Maybe you have wasted mercy.
Maybe you have repeatedly asked God for things while refusing the God who gave them.
Still…
the cross stands.
The tomb is empty.
Grace is being offered.
And Jesus is still rewriting people.
So open your hands.
But first…
open your heart.
Because the hands pierced open for you are the reason your hands can finally open for someone else.
